transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-29
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (GrooveWorks Head of AI), Carlos Mendoza (Infra), Anya Ivanov (Product)

Quick Summary:
GrooveWorks is preparing a 6-week pilot to validate latency and cost for their conversational assistant. Main focus: define TTFT (time-to-first-token) and TPOT (time-per-token) SLOs, sampling plan across request sizes and burst patterns, and decide whether to run the benchmark on Redwood hosted or Dedicated capacity. Action items assigned for SOW, benchmark configs, and data handoff.

Topics covered:
- Success criteria and acceptance thresholds (p95/p99 for TTFT and TPOT)
- Workload sizing: RPS, median/95th sequence lengths, burst factors
- Measurement plan: sampling buckets, run cadence, client-side vs server-side measurement alignment
- Infrastructure choices: hosted vs dedicated, VPC/network constraints, profiling kernels/quantization
- Next steps and deliverables

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Ok, everyone thanks for joining. We're gonna run through scope and make sure we have clear pass/fail for the pilot. Priya, do you want to kick off with what success looks like for GrooveWorks?
[00:00:14] Priya (GrooveWorks): Sure, yeah. So we ship a chat assistant in product and the two things we care about are latency for live users and the per-token cost because we're cost-sensitive. Success = comparable latency to our current in-house endpoints at 95th percentile and lower unit cost or a clear path to it. Timeline wise we want to start running benchmarks in the next two weeks.
[00:00:35] Maya: Great — that's the two knobs we typically tune: TTFT and TPOT. Liam will walk through measurement details.
[00:00:42] Liam (Redwood SE): Hey all. Quick framing: TTFT is the wall-clock from request arrival to first token emitted. TPOT is essentially average time per token for generation after the first token. For SLOs we recommend separate p95/p99 targets for each because they affect different UX behaviors — TTFT hits perceived responsiveness, TPOT affects long responses and throughput cost.
[00:01:03] Carlos (Infra): Just clarifying: our current baseline is roughly 180ms p95 for first byte at 1x load but that was on a smaller model and with a custom batching layer. Under peak traffic we see spikes to 1.8s at p99. We want realistic traffic shapes in the test.
[00:01:22] Priya: Yep. Median sequence length is about 64 tokens; 95th is 420; we have occasional long tails up to 1,024 tokens for doc-summaries. Traffic avg is 200 RPS across global region with bursts to 2k for brief events.
[00:01:39] Liam: Cool — good numbers. For the pilot we should model three buckets: short (<=64), mid (65-512), long (>512). Each bucket will have separate TTFT/TPOT targets and sampling ratios.
[00:01:55] Anya (Product): Can you recommend what sampling ratios we should use? Most of our users are short but the long ones are critical.
[00:02:03] Liam: I'd suggest 75% short, 20% mid, 5% long for steady-state. For burst testing, scale the short bucket up to simulate 5x-10x short-request spikes; keep long ones at the same absolute numbers since those are rare but heavy.
[00:02:17] Priya: Makes sense. For SLO numbers, I want to propose TTFT p95 = 250ms, p99 = 600ms for steady state. TPOT p95 = 40ms/token and p99 = 100ms/token. Are those realistic for you?
[00:02:32] Liam: They might be ambitious for hosted without dedicated GPUs depending on model. What model family are you planning to use? Priya?
[00:02:39] Priya: We're testing on the open Llama-variant we use in-house, roughly 30B parameters quantized to 4-bit in production.
[00:02:47] Liam: Ok, that helps. With 30B quantized to 4-bit on dedicated A100-equivalent GPUs we can likely hit TTFT p95 ~120-160ms for short requests and TPOT p95 ~20-30ms/token. On hosted smaller infer nodes or CPU fallbacks, TTFT could be 300-600ms. So we should make two acceptance tracks: hosted SLO (less strict) and dedicated SLO (target optimum).
[00:03:09] Maya: Good call. Let's draft the SLO table in the doc. Example: Short bucket (<=64): Dedicated TTFT p95 140ms, p99 320ms; Hosted TTFT p95 280ms, p99 700ms. TPOT targets same pattern. We'll put exact numbers in the shared spreadsheet.
[00:03:27] Carlos: How do you measure TTFT precisely? Our current instrumentation is inconsistent between client and server.
[00:03:33] Liam: We run both client-side synthetic load (to simulate network, TLS, etc.) and a server-side probe that measures processing time from request dequeue to token emit. For SLOs we align them: client-measured TTFT = network+routing+server_dequeue+first_token. We'll provide a measurement harness — the load agent will emit both timings so we can decompose where time is spent.
[00:03:54] Priya: Is the load agent available as a repo? We prefer something we can run in our infra for dedicated runs.
[00:03:59] Liam: Yes — we'll share the benchmark repo. It has configs for sequence distributions, burst shaping, open-loop vs closed-loop, and sample payload scrapers.
[00:04:08] Anya: For cost measurement — TPOT maps to tokens/sec which maps to GPU utilization and then cost. How do you map tokens to per-req cost when responses vary in length?
[00:04:17] Maya: We compute per-request cost = tokens_generated * unit_cost_per_token + fixed_request_overhead. For pilot we'll standardize on a few representative prompts so we can show a cost-per-session curve.
[00:04:29] Priya: Ok. On infra: we will likely need VPC peering for Dedicated; our security team requires no egress to the public internet for payloads. Is that supported?
[00:04:38] Maya: Absolutely — Redwood Private supports customer-managed VPC peering or on-prem connector. For the pilot we can start with Dedicated in a private VPC. We'll send the network diagram and required firewall ports.
[00:04:49] Carlos: Any gotchas with HSM/KMS for keys? Our keys need to stay in our KMS for compliance.
[00:04:54] Liam: We can integrate with customer KMS/HSM for model keys and sign-off. We'll include the KMS integration steps in the security pack.
[00:05:01] Priya: Back to SLOs — how do you handle batching & KV cache effects in measurement? Our in-house system has aggressive prefix caching which helps TTFT for repeated prompts.
[00:05:09] Liam: Good point. We'll run tests with cache-warm and cache-cold scenarios. For TTFT SLOs we define two modes: cold-first (no cache) and warm (50% cache hit rate). We'll also control batching window in the benchmark so you can see tradeoffs between latency and throughput.
[00:05:24] Anya: Will the benchmark show end-to-end percentiles across regions? We have global traffic.
[00:05:29] Maya: We'll run geo-distributed agents or use Redwood hosted endpoints in target regions to capture network tail. We'll include p50/p95/p99 for both client and server metrics by region.
[00:05:40] Carlos: For the p99 numbers, do you recommend any error budget? How much leeway should product accept?
[00:05:47] Liam: Typical error budgets for p99 in pilots are 1-5% depending on criticality. For GrooveWorks, since this is a user-facing chat, I'd recommend a 2% error budget for p99 over a 30-day window if you want stable UX. For pilot we'll use sampling windows (2-hour runs) and extrapolate.
[00:06:02] Priya: Ok. We also need to understand model fallbacks. If the preferred model isn't available, we want graceful degradation to a faster smaller model — how does Redwood handle that in SLOs?
[00:06:12] Liam: We support automatic fallback policies. For SLO acceptance we'll define allowed fallback tiers and SLO multipliers (e.g., if fallback to 7B occurs, TTFT allowed to be x2 and TPOT x1.5). Those fallbacks will be reported separately in the benchmark.
[00:06:26] Maya: Cool. Let's cover the concrete measurement plan now. Liam?
[00:06:29] Liam: Measurement plan (high level):
- Phase 0: Data handoff (GrooveWorks provides 30K representative requests and sequence length histogram).
- Phase 1: Dry run on Redwood hosted small cluster to validate harness and sampling (1 hour).
- Phase 2: Dedicated baseline runs (3 x 2-hour sweeps) across short/mid/long buckets, including cache-cold and cache-warm.
- Phase 3: Burst resilience tests with 5x and 10x short-request spikes, measure tail amplification and degradation path.
- Phase 4: Cost projection and per-session cost curve; show tradeoffs with batching/quantization.

[00:07:05] Priya: How do you pick the hardware for Dedicated? We have a procurement constraint but can commit to a monthly reserved capacity.
[00:07:12] Liam: For 30B 4-bit we recommend an A100 or equivalent with adequate memory for KV cache; baseline pilot with 2 GPUs will show per-GPU throughput. We'll run scaling tests to map GPUs -> RPS and produce a sizing table.
[00:07:25] Carlos: We'll also want to know what autoscaling policies look like during spikes so we don't overprovision.
[00:07:29] Maya: Redwood Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling and burst capacity; we'll include recommended policies in the SOW draft.
[00:07:35] Anya: For acceptance, do we require both TTFT and TPOT to be within targets, or is it ok if one misses slightly?
[00:07:41] Liam: Recommend a pass/fail matrix: primary metric = TTFT p95 (user perception), secondary = TPOT p95 and cost-per-session. To pass pilot, short bucket TTFT p95 must meet dedicated or hosted target per selected track, and overall cost-per-session must be within agreed range. We can allow up to 3% p99 breaches on a run for experimental reasons but not for acceptance.
[00:08:00] Priya: Good. One more question: how will you attribute latency spikes to network vs server?
[00:08:04] Liam: The benchmark agent emits client RTT, server processing start/emit times, and we instrument kernel-level traces on the runtime side for GPU stalls and batching delays. We'll provide decomposed latency waterfall charts.
[00:08:18] Carlos: Sounds comprehensive. On the security doc, we need to see audit log retention and RBAC details.
[00:08:23] Maya: We'll include audit log retention options and RBAC roles in the security pack.
[00:08:28] Priya: Ok, timeline recap?
[00:08:31] Maya: Action items we already noted — quick timeline: data handoff by 2026-11-01, benchmark config and run ready by 2026-11-02, first hosted dry run 2026-11-04, dedicated runs scheduled 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-11, SOW signed by 2026-11-12 ideally.
[00:08:48] Priya: That timeline works for us.
[00:08:50] Anya: Anything else on metrics? We also want memory/kv cache hit rates and batching windows in the report.
[00:08:55] Liam: Yes — each run includes per-shard GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, batching stats (avg batch size, batching latency), p50/p95/p99 TTFT & TPOT, and cost projection.
[00:09:08] Maya: Ok, let's do a quick example SLO table verbally — we will formalize it in the doc: Short requests <=64 tokens: Dedicated TTFT p95 140ms, p99 350ms; TPOT p95 25ms/token, p99 65ms/token. Hosted TTFT p95 300ms, p99 800ms; TPOT p95 45ms/token, p99 120ms/token. Mid requests 65-512: Dedicated TTFT p95 160ms, p99 420ms; TPOT p95 30ms/token. Long requests >512: accept higher TTFT and per-token times, but measure end-to-end stability.
[00:09:44] Priya: Those Dedicated numbers look good. We'll start with the Dedicated track for acceptance if the pricing works out.
[00:09:50] Carlos: On the pricing, can you provide an example cost projection for 200 RPS avg and peak 2k?
[00:09:56] Maya: We'll attach cost projection examples in the SOW with per-GPU throughput and cost. For the pilot we will run actual utilization numbers and produce a real projection.
[00:10:04] Priya: Perfect.
[00:10:06] Maya: Anything else?
[00:10:07] Priya: One small ask: please include the fallback behavior report as part of the run, especially how latency backoffs are handled.
[00:10:12] Liam: Noted — we'll include a fallback-run where we force a model fallback and measure UX degradation, plus a run with circuit-breaker behavior when queue depth exceeds threshold.
[00:10:23] Carlos: That should help our SREs sign off.
[00:10:26] Maya: Alright, quick recap of next steps: Maya sends SOW + pricing + security pack; Liam sends benchmark repo + config; GrooveWorks to share payloads and network info. We'll reconvene after the hosted dry run to review results.
[00:10:41] Priya: Thanks, everyone.
[00:10:42] Anya: Thanks.
[00:10:43] Liam: Thanks all.

Notes about transcription quality and artifacts:
- Occasional mis-hear: "KV cache" rendered as "K V cash" in some auto-frames; speaker labels may have brief misattribution on overlapping talk.

End meeting.
